title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
An AI-generated deepfake article impersonated an ABC finance presenter and a Reserve Bank governor to promote an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The fabricated interview was deployed online as a scam artifact alongside fake news articles, reviews, and websites designed to build credibility for the fraudulent scheme. This represents a failure of content moderation systems and AI safeguards that allowed generative systems to be misused for impersonation at scale.

The deployment happened across multiple web platforms that hosted the fake content without verification. It would have taken identity verification checks, cross-referencing against official public records, and human review of high-stakes financial content to catch and remove this before it reached potential victims. ASIC reports this type of AI-enabled impersonation scam is becoming increasingly common and sophisticated, with scammers targeting prime ministers, politicians, financial experts, and wealthy individuals.

It is not established how the AI systems used to generate the deepfakes were obtained, trained, or whether their creators intended them for this purpose.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article featuring ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock illustrates a rising type of scam. The fabricated interview depicted Bullock storming out over Kohler's questions about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The interview never occurred. ASIC reports this type of scam using AI-generated deepfakes of celebrities and politicians is becoming increasingly common and sophisticated. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is the most frequently impersonated public figure, followed by politicians like Angus Taylor and Pauline Hanson, along with financial experts and wealthy individuals including Gina Rinehart.

Last year, ASIC removed 19,400 scams overall, representing a 182 percent increase. Phishing scams jumped 279 percent with 5,476 removed, while fake investment platforms surged 151 percent to 7,051 takedowns. Scammers now build elaborate webs of deception using fake news articles, reviews, and websites. ASIC urges consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing. Presenter Kohler argues stronger penalties for platforms and AI models hosting fraudulent content are necessary beyond simply warning consumers.
